extracted.intended_audience: editors and journalism educators (teachers of basic newswriting/reporting)
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive study of how undergraduate basic newswriting and reporting courses are taught at accredited journalism schools: course placement, instructor background, content emphases, lab practices, processing of student copy, and evaluation methods. Intended to inform editors and educators about prevailing practices and suggested improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course placement/level
rubrics_metrics.description: At what level the course is listed in the catalog (freshman, sophomore, junior, senior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most respondents reported the basic newswriting/reporting course is a sophomore-level offering (78% sophomore, 18% junior, 4% freshman). None listed it as senior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course duration/term structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the course is offered as a one-semester, one-quarter, two-quarter package, or full-year sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Majority offered one-term: 54% one-semester, 31% one-quarter, 3% two-quarter package, 12% full-year sequence. Use this to plan pacing and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course availability/frequency per academic year
rubrics_metrics.description: How many times the course is offered during an academic year (counting separate offerings/sections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses varied widely (1–2 times: 17%; 3–5: 20%; 6–10: 38%; >10: 25%). Some schools offer many sections for large enrollments; availability affects access and scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic credit allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Total academic credit assigned to the course (converted to quarter hours for comparison).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common allocations: 3 quarter hours (12%), 4 quarter hours (18%), 4.5 quarter hours (45%), 5 quarter hours (7%), 6 (6%), >6 (12%). Credit weighting situates the course within degree requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor professional journalistic experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Years of full-time professional journalism experience held by the instructor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Profile: 0% none, 7% up to 2 years, 20% 2–5 years, 25% 5–10 years, 25% 10–15 years, 23% >15 years. Many instructors bring substantial newsroom experience; this is considered valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor teaching experience and academic rank/degree
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructor's years of teaching experience, academic rank, and highest earned degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching experience groups: 0–2 years 7%, 3–5:18%, 5–10:32%, 10–15:18%, >15:25%. Ranks: instructor 3%, asst prof 34%, assoc prof 32%, prof 30%. Degrees: none 4%, bachelor 8%, master 46%, doctorate 42%. Use instructor qualifications to assess course leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of assistance/teaching staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether principal instructor typically has assistance and the source (faculty, grad TAs, undergrad TAs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 76% reported no assistance; 24% did. Of those assisted: 40% other faculty, 43% graduate teaching fellows, 17% undergraduate TAs. Only ~14% rely on TAs; many courses taught primarily by principal instructor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of instructor's course load represented by the basic course
rubrics_metrics.description: Share of a faculty member’s total teaching load the basic course represents (e.g., 1/3, 1/2, entire load).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses: 1/4 load 19%, 1/3 51%, 1/2 21%, 2/3 4%, entire load 5%. For many instructors the basic course is a substantial part of load, often with multiple sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non-academic professionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how instructors use local press professionals in the course (guest lecturers, interview subjects, paid vs. unpaid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 57% used professionals, typically as guest lecturers (49%) or interview subjects (38%); 80% of professionals unpaid. Professionals sometimes teach labs or full offerings when on payroll.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture hours per week
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical class hours per week allocated to lecture/discussion in the course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribution: 1 hour 25%, 2 hours 50%, 3 hours 16%, 4 hours 5%, 5 hours 3%, >6 hours 1%. Balance lecture vs. lab affects hands-on practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory hours per week
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical class hours per week allocated to laboratory sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribution: 1 hour 7%, 2 hours 31%, 3 hours 26%, 4 hours 24%, 5 hours 6%, 6 hours 3%, >6 hours 3%. Lab time is central to practical skills development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lab class size / accreditation expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended/typical enrollment in laboratory sections and accreditation concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported lab sizes: <15 students 19%, 15–20 45%, 21–25 14%, 26–30 4%, 31–35 2%, 36–40 5%, >40 11%. Accreditation teams often criticize labs >15–20; 36% reported labs >20.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary and supplementary texts/resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of required primary text(s) and supplementary texts (style guides, workbooks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most-cited primary texts: Macdougall's Interpretative Reporting (27), Charnley Reporting (24), Hohenberg's The Professional Journalist (11), Vizard/Culbertson/Lambert (10). Supplementary: AP-UPI Stylebook (38), The Elements of Style (17). Ten instructors used no primary text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture topic emphases — news gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of emphasis given to news gathering techniques in lecture/discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 76% gave 'a great deal' or 'quite a lot' of emphasis. News gathering is a central lecture topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture topic emphases — news writing techniques (story structure, transitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis on story structure and transitions in lecture/discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 95% gave 'a great deal' or 'quite a lot' — regarded as fundamental lecture content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture topic emphases — lead writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis on lead-writing skills in lectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 87% gave 'a great deal' or 'quite a lot'. Lead writing is a core skill emphasized heavily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture topic emphases — news writing style (readability, clarity, sentence length)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis on style, readability and clarity in lecture/discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 93% gave 'a great deal' or 'quite a lot'. Style is universally emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture topic emphases — interviewing techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis on conducting interviews effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 64% 'a great deal', 27% 'some' — included in most courses but somewhat less emphasized than structure/style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture topic emphases — legal hazards (libel, privacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction on legal risks such as libel and invasion of privacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 19% 'a great deal', 52% 'some', 29% 'almost none'. Some programs separate law into distinct courses, reducing lecture-time here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture topic emphases — diction and syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on word choice (diction) and sentence construction (syntax) in lectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction: 60% 'a great deal', 30% 'some'; Syntax: 65% 'a great deal', 25% 'some'. Both are standard lecture elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture topic emphases — spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis placed on correct spelling in lectures/discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 66% 'a great deal', 24% 'some'. Spelling is still a notable focus despite being considered basic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture topic emphases — news judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching how to recognize and prioritize news values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 90% 'a great deal' or 'quite a lot'. News judgment is a central lecture objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture topic emphases — ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction in journalistic ethics in lectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 53% 'a great deal', 32% 'some', 15% 'almost none'. Ethics included but sometimes covered in other courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of simulated versus actual news situations in labs
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequency of using standardized simulated situations, campus events, off-campus events, and beat assignments in lab work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simulated lab situations used frequently (32% 'often', 25% 'sometimes'); campus events used but less often; off-campus events and beats much less used. Many instructors rely on controlled/simulated exercises rather than real beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for setting up simulated news situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques used to create simulated news situations in lab: handouts, workbooks, instructor/TA simulations, role-play, audio/video, outside guests, dictated details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most common: dittoed handouts (used by many). Published workbooks declined. Instructor-simulated sources, instructor dictation, audio tapes used to varying degrees; video tapes and programmed instruction were rare due to cost. Teaching assistants rarely role-play sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lab problem focus areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific problems exercises are designed to emphasize (e.g., assessing news values, accuracy, dealing with quotes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top-ranked emphases (number of respondents): assessing news values (85), accuracy (82), dealing with quotes (76), organizing complex details (75), avoidance of libel (59), organizing action sequences (53), balance (48), avoidance of reporter bias (45), taste (41), avoidance of invasion of privacy (15). Other recurring emphases: attribution, clarity, conciseness, deadline pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outside reporting assignment types and frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Kinds of off-lab news situations assigned (campus meetings, speeches, student government, downtown beats/interviews) and how frequently they are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors rely heavily on on-campus events (meetings, speeches); downtown beat coverage is seldom used. Tables show many instructors prefer events that are easy to monitor and grade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and type of writing assignments per term
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical volume of writing assignments students complete during a single term and their scope (single-lab vs. multi-period/investigative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counts: <10 (3%), 10–19 (17%), 20–29 (36%), 30–39 (16%), 40+ (23%). Most assignments are single-lab deadline pieces, though some assignments span multiple labs and result in investigative series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing of student copy — editing and return
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which student assignments are edited, corrected, and handed back to students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 89% indicated that nearly all assignments are edited and returned. This suggests minimal writing is discarded without feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing of student copy — who edits
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of editing/corrections performed by the principal instructor versus others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 80% of corrected/edited assignments are handled by the principal instructor for the course. Indicates heavy instructor involvement in feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grading coverage of assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of total writing assignments that receive a grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: About half indicated most assignments are graded (49% in highest category); practices vary—some use grades sparingly except for final grade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class-wide critique practices
rubrics_metrics.description: How often assignments are critiqued/discussed for the benefit of the whole class and by which methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approaches among those who critique: instructor reads copy aloud noting corrections (69%), transparencies (41%), corrected stories dittoed/distributed (34%), uncorrected stories distributed and corrected in discussion (18%), corrected stories left in open file (6%). Instructors differed on whether to critique publicly or give only individual feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: How quickly edited and graded copy is returned to students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Returned before next class 10%, at next meeting 57%, within a week 28%, within two weeks 3%, next scheduled individual conference 2%. Majority return feedback promptly (next meeting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for communicating criticisms and suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms used to communicate instructor/TA critiques (marginal comments, conferences, written critiques, checklists, computerized exercises).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices: marginal comments/editing on original copy 97%, individual conferences 81%, extensive written critiques 42%, standardized checklist 8%, computerized exercises 1%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual conferences — frequency and duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of individual conferences per student per term and typical length of each conference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Among those using conferences: one 5%, two 15%, three 17%, four 7%, five 1%, six 1%, varies remainder. Duration: ≤10 min 10%, 10–15 min 36%, 15–30 min 34%, >30 min 4%, varies 17%. Instructors noted effectiveness depends on depth of conferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite requirement and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequency with which students are required to rewrite copy (as pedagogical tool).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy returned to student to be rewritten: often (18%), sometimes (59%), seldom (12%), never (11%). Several instructors required multiple rewrites until professional standard reached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of student work
rubrics_metrics.description: How frequently student copy is published in lab publications, campus papers/magazines, or off-campus outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lab publication: rare (0% often, 9% sometimes); campus paper: varied (10% often, 28% sometimes); off-campus publications: uncommon (3% often, 21% sometimes). Many instructors advocated more publication to give students media experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grading emphasis — factors considered in evaluating writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative importance placed on specific factors when grading student writing assignments (news values, style, accuracy, spelling, diction, syntax, transitions, originality, leads, organization, completeness, fairness, handling of quotes, avoidance of jargon, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High emphasis items: recognition of news values 95% 'a great deal', writing style 100%, accuracy 100%, spelling 88%, diction 78%, syntax 78%, transitions 71%, originality 62%, lead devices 81%, organization 94%, completeness 92%, fairness 91%, handling of quotes 88%, avoidance of jargon 67%. Additional written-in factors: enterprise, deadlines, adherence to style, brevity, making it interesting, 'serving the truth'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination approaches for evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of exam or testing methods used to assess student achievement (standardized lab exercises, midterm, final, spot quizzes, current events quizzes, away-from-lab assignments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used methods: standardized lab exercises 52%, midterm 45%, final 44%, spot quizzes 34%, current events quizzes 32%, away-from-lab assignments 15%. Many instructors use multiple exam types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common problems/constraints in achieving course objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: List of chief problems instructors cited: poorly motivated students, inadequate English/grammar background, insufficient time, class sizes too large, lack of equipment/labs, difficulty getting students interested, varying student levels in same class, lack of assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most frequently cited issues: poor student motivation/weak English (37 mentions), insufficient time (29), large classes (19), inadequate equipment (8). These constraints inform recommended remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested course improvements / best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors’ suggestions to improve the basic course (more individual work, fewer contrived situations, adopt new techniques, weed out misfits, publish student work, reduce class size, more rewriting, more newsgathering, team-teaching, small honors sections, off-campus field trips).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top suggestions: more individual conferences (19 mentions); move away from contrived handouts (16); adapt to programmed instruction/video (9); use entrance exams (8); get more student work into print (8); cut down class size (6); emphasize doing/field work over lectures (6); require more rewriting and news gathering. Several recommend team-teaching and limiting enrollment for honors sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical philosophy / instructor practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative practices and philosophies emphasized: quick establishment of editor-to-reporter rapport, blend of toughness and concern, intensive margin comments, early field work, classroom critique for shared learning, insistence on professional standards and rewrites, team teaching and close student-instructor ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excerpts and anecdotes illustrate practices: insist rewrite until professional standard attained; team-taught half-day small sections (ratio 1:10) build morale; staged unfolding stories to create realism; honors sections for advanced students with field trips to legislature. These are presented as effective instructional patterns.
